Background:
The COVID-19 pandemic brought serious consequences for global public health and revealed deep inequalities in the impact of the disease on different social groups. Since its emergence in late 2019, COVID-19 has affected millions of people worldwide, with varying magnitudes of morbidity and mortality rates across countries. While many individuals recover within a relatively short period of time, a significant portion develop a post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), characterized by the ‘persistence or emergence of new symptoms at least three months following the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, lasting for a minimum of two months without an alternative explanation’ [ 1–3 ]. The World Health Organization (WHO) has highlighted the importance of recognizing these long-term effects as being critical to understanding the full impact of the pandemic on health systems and populations [ 1 ].

In Brazil—a country marked by stark social inequalities—the COVID-19 pandemic has been particularly severe, being responsible for ∼700 000 deaths, which is the second-largest absolute mortality among all countries [ 4 , 5 ]. Social and economic factors, such as gender, ethnicity, and wealth, may have influenced the severity of the COVID-19 episode and the likelihood of developing PCC. Studies indicate that racial and ethnic minorities, particularly Black and Indigenous populations, have faced disproportionate impacts due to pre-existing health disparities, occupational exposures, and systemic inequities in healthcare access [ 6 , 7 ]. Furthermore, the Brazilian healthcare system has been challenged by the long-term symptoms associated with PCC, which include fatigue, headaches, and mental health issues such as anxiety and depression, significantly affecting patients’ quality of life and straining existing resources. Understanding the factors associated with symptom persistence among individuals with COVID-19 and PCC is crucial for better targeting prevention and intervention strategies that account for the vulnerability of different population groups [ 8 , 9 ].

In 2020, the Epicovid study relied upon four nationwide, population-based samples to track the progression of the COVID-19 pandemic throughout Brazil [ 10 , 11 ] in 133 sentinel cities. In the present investigation—Epicovid 2.0—we used the same sampling methodology to provide insights into the prevalence and persistence of symptoms related to COVID-19 in the country, focusing on PCC and also comparing the experiences of individuals with and without reported COVID-19 episodes. By evaluating these symptoms, we seek to enhance the understanding of the challenges faced by the Brazilian healthcare system and by the country as a whole in addressing the long-term effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Methods:
The Epicovid 2.0 survey was carried out between March and June 2024, covering all 26 states of the country and the Federal District. The Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) divides the country into 133 intermediate regions and the largest city in each of these regions was included in the survey. The survey used a multistage probabilistic sampling method. In each city, 25 urban census tracts were selected, with sampling probability proportionate to their size. Ten households were randomly chosen from each census tract, resulting in 250 households per city. In each household, one person was randomly chosen to participate, with a second person selected if the first declined. If both refused, then the team moved on to the next neighbouring household. If a household contained only one person who refused, then the team proceeded to the next household. The target sample size for the study was 33 250 individuals.

This study was approved by the School of Physical Education Ethics Committee at the Federal University of Pelotas (CAAE: 68382923.8.0000.5313). Participants signed an informed consent form if they were ≥18 years old. For those below this age, the responsible caregiver signed on their behalf. Confidentiality was ensured.

### Outcomes

The main study outcomes were the presence of the following symptoms in the 3 months before the interview: (i) tiredness, (ii) shortness of breath, (iii) anosmia, (iv) cough, (v) difficulties in concentrating, (vi) body pain, (vii) joint pain, (viii) headache, (ix) chest pain, (x) tachycardia, (xi) memory loss, (xii) anxiety, (xiii) dizziness, (xiv) difficulties in moving, (xv) difficulties in standing up, (xvi) skin spots, (xvii) loss of appetite, (xviii) diarrhoea, (xix) sleep problems, (xx) loss of hands sensitivity, and (xxi) problems in menstruation (for women). Each symptom was recorded as never, less than once a month, one to three times a month, at least weekly, and daily. For ease of interpretation, we dichotomize each symptom, with ‘yes’ recorded in the presence of the symptom, regardless of its frequency. We assessed each symptom separately and also a sum of symptoms.

We also investigated the presence of PCC. Respondents were asked ‘Have you ever had COVID-19?’ and, for those with a positive answer, the number of episodes was recorded. Among individuals who self-reported one or more episodes, we relied upon the WHO PCC definition, asking them the following question: ‘During the three months after your COVID-19 episode, did you present any of the following symptoms for at least two months?’ Respondents were prompted for the same 21 symptoms listed above and their replies were used to generate the PCC variable according to the WHO definition. If more than one episode of COVID-19 was reported, all symptoms following one or more episodes were considered. We then used the answers to create a variable with three categories: no history of COVID-19, COVID-19 history without PCC, and COVID-19 history with PCC.

### Stratification variables

Results were stratified by country region, age, sex, skin colour, schooling, wealth index, and at least one COVID-19 infection. The country regions include the North, Northeast, Southeast, South, and Center-West. Age in complete years was stratified into eight groups: 0–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, and ≥80 years. Biological sex was recorded as male and female. The assessment of self-reported race or skin colour followed the nationally standardized (IBGE) definition: White, Brown, Black, Asian, and Indigenous. The number of completed years of formal schooling was recorded and grouped as 0–4, 5–8, 9–11, and ≥12. A wealth index was generated through principal component analysis based upon several household assets and characteristics. The first component was extracted and then divided into quintiles, with the first quintile being the 20% poorer individuals. Further details of the methodology and analyses are presented elsewhere [ 12 ].

### Statistical analyses

All analyses were performed by using Stata New 18.1 (StataCorp, 2023, Stata Statistical Software: Release 18, College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC). Descriptive analyses included calculating proportions or averages [with their respective 95% confidence interval (CI)] according to the nature of the outcome. We ran bivariate analyses of the outcomes for each explanatory variable. The heterogeneity chi-squared and student’s t or analyses of variance (ANOVA) tests were used.

We used sampling weights to adjust for non-response. Specifically, we aligned the distribution of sex, age, and ethnicity for each of the 133 cities in our survey with the corresponding distributions reported by the national 2022 census [ 13 ]. City population size was also factored in by dividing the census-based results by the number of interviews conducted in each city. These ratios were then multiplied to derive the final survey weights. Once the weights were calculated, we defined the survey design in Stata by using the ‘svyset’ command, with the city as the stratification variable and the census sector as the primary sampling unit. All subsequent analyses were performed by using the ‘svy’ command in Stata, which adjusted for the complex survey design by accounting for stratification, clustering, and within-city correlations.
Results:
Among the randomly selected individuals, 92.5% agreed to participate in the study. The sample comprised 33 250 respondents, of whom almost one-third lived in the Northeast region and one-quarter in the Southeast. More than half were females and had ≥9 years of schooling. Regarding age, almost half of those interviewed were in the 40–69 years group, while 12% were aged ≥70 years. Regarding race or skin colour, 49% reported being Brown and 33% White ( Table 1 ). The overall frequencies of symptoms in the 3 months before the interview, regardless of COVID-19 history, are presented in Supplementary Table 1 . The most frequent symptoms were headache (46.3%), followed by anxiety (45.4%) and tiredness (38.8%).

### COVID-19 history and average number of symptoms

COVID-19 history was reported by 28.6% (95% CI 27.3 to 30.0) of the sampled individuals ( Table 1 ), with the highest prevalence observed in the North and South regions, in individuals aged 30–49 years, and among females, Whites, and Asians. The prevalence increased monotonically with schooling and wealth levels. The average number of symptoms in the 3 months before the interview was 3.46 (95% CI 3.32 to 3.60) in the whole sample. Means were higher in the North and Southeast regions, among individuals aged ≥80 years, and among females and Indigenous individuals. Low schooling and poverty were associated with fewer reported symptoms ( Table 1 ).

Figure 1 shows the average number of symptoms according to COVID-19 history, also stratified by categories of the explanatory variables. On average, individuals with a COVID-19 history presented 5.0 symptoms (95% CI 4.76 to 5.24)—almost double the average of those without a history (average = 2.77; 95% CI 2.62 to 2.92). This pattern was observed in all categories of all explanatory variables, except among individuals aged ≥80 years. The widest gaps were observed for Indigenous people, females, and in the poorest quintiles ( Figure 1 ).

### PCC prevalence

Around two-thirds (65.1%; 95% CI 62.7 to 67.4) of individuals with a history of COVID-19 presented PCC. This represents 18.0% (95% CI 16.9 to 19.2) of all individuals interviewed. Among those with a history of PCC, ∼4 in every 10 individuals (44.2%; 95% CI 40.1 to 48.3) still presented the symptoms at the time of assessment. PCC was more frequent among Indigenous people, females, and individuals aged 20–59 years, and lower among those with zero to 4 years of schooling ( Figure 2 ).

PCC prevalence was studied according to episode severity. Among patients who were not hospitalized, the prevalence was 64.2% (95% CI 61.7 to 66.6); among the hospitalized who did not require oxygen, it was 71.7% (95% CI 56.9 to 82.9); and among those who required oxygen support or were intubated, the PCC prevalence was 85.3% (95% CI 79.6 to 89.7).

### Symptoms by COVID-19/PCC history

The prevalence of each symptom in the 3 months before the interview is shown in Figure 3 for individuals without a history of COVID-19, with COVID-19 history without PCC, and with COVID-19 history with PCC. Because PCC is defined based on recent symptomatology, it is not surprising that this category shows higher frequencies than the other two groups. The differences are particularly large for memory loss, hair loss, difficulty in concentration, joint pains, tiredness, and anxiety (see Supplementary Table S1 for more details).

To assess how common recent symptoms are related to COVID-19 history, Figure 4 plots the full-sample prevalence of each symptom against their prevalence ratio by comparing individuals with and without a COVID-19 history. For example, headaches show a high prevalence in the sample, but this symptom is only ∼50% more common in those who suffered from COVID-19 than among those who did not, while memory loss has a lower overall prevalence (∼15%), but is three times as common in individuals with a COVID-19 history. In addition to memory loss, individuals with a COVID-19 history were substantially more likely to report anosmia, loss of sensitivity in the hands, difficulty in concentration, and hair loss ( Figure 4 ). Similar patterns were observed among those with PCC compared with the rest of the sample, with slightly higher prevalence ratios for all symptoms ( Supplementary Figure S1 ).

Building upon the results presented in Figure 1 to also incorporate PCC status, the average number of reported symptoms was 2.77 (95% CI 2.62 to 2.92) among those without a COVID-19 history, 2.17 (95% CI 1.99 to 2.35) among those who had an episode but did not develop PCC, 6.04 (95% CI 5.69 to 6.40) among those with PCC in the past, and 7.21 (95% CI 6.73 to 7.69) among those with current PCC. These differences are illustrated in the Sankey plot shown in Figure 5 .
Discussion:
COVID-19 history was reported by about one in four participants. Among these individuals, two-thirds had PCC. The symptoms evaluated were more frequent in those with a history of COVID-19, especially among those with PCC and persistent symptoms. Our findings are similar to those already described in the literature. It is estimated that PCC affects 20%–30% of the population with a history of COVID-19 [ 14 ]. A systematic review of 48 studies showed that the prevalence of PCC ranged from ∼3% to 90%, with 41.3% (95% CI 39.3 to 43.4) having symptoms lasting for ≥12 months [ 15 ]. No relevant variations in PCC prevalence were observed according to the regions analysed (Europe, Americas, Asia, Africa, and Australia). Another study found that the pooled prevalence of PCC was 43% (95% CI 39% to 46%, including 33 studies), with higher rates in hospitalized patients compared with non-hospitalized patients [ 16 ]—a finding that we also observed in our sample.

In Brazil, the waves of COVID-19 hit the country differently. The first rounds of the Epicovid study showed that, when the pandemic started in 2020, the North region (Amazon) presented the highest antibody seroprevalence against SARS-CoV-2, followed by large metropolises such as São Paulo and Rio [ 11 ]. The second wave (late 2020 to mid-2021) spread broadly, with major impacts in the Amazon and in the South, driven by the Gamma variant that caused high mortality rates [ 17 ]. The third wave (mid-2021 to early 2022) saw new variants across Brazil, with vaccinations mitigating severe outcomes, particularly in South and Southeastern regions such as São Paulo. Subsequent waves, influenced by variants such as Omicron, led to high transmission, but were less severe due to increasing vaccination rates.

In our study, the occurrence of symptoms showed small variability across regions. We also showed that headaches, anxiety, fatigue, and cough were the most prevalent symptoms in the sample. These were the most common symptoms in those with PCC except for cough. Additionally, concentration difficulties, body aches, and memory and hair loss were also notable among those with PCC. A review indicated that the most common symptoms in individuals with a history of COVID-19 were fatigue (23%), memory loss (14%), shortness of breath (13%), sleep problems (11%), and joint pain (10%) [ 16 ]. These symptoms in individuals with a history of COVID-19, especially those with PCC, may be explained by neuroinflammatory changes in peripheral nerves, damage to blood vessels due to clotting and endothelial dysfunction, and neuronal damage after the COVID-19 episode [ 18 , 19 ]. Moreover, COVID-19 history may lead to immune system dysregulation, microbiota dysbiosis, dysfunctional neurological signalling, and endothelial abnormalities. All these changes may trigger many of the observed symptoms [ 19 ].

The occurrence of multiple symptoms in people with a history of COVID-19 was higher in all categories assessed, especially among women and Indigenous people. Women and girls have a higher risk of PCC and, consequently, of experiencing symptoms [ 14 ]. Some studies suggest that hormonal factors maintain a hyperinflammatory state in women [ 20 , 21 ]. However, it is also known that women are better at recognizing symptoms than men, which may also result in the underreporting of symptoms among men. Regarding Indigenous people, the first Epicovid survey [ 11 ] already showed that they were the group with the highest SARS-CoV-2 infection rate. However, few studies have addressed the occurrence of PCC according to Indigenous ethnicity. To date, a PubMed search using the terms (‘Indigenous’ OR ‘indígena’) AND (‘post COVID-19 condition’ OR ‘long COVID’) identified only three references, none of which assessed associations between being Indigenous and having PCC. Healthcare systems must not leave vulnerable communities behind when ensuring effective strategies for managing PCC and related symptoms [ 22 ].

Diagnosing PCC is a challenge worldwide, especially in Brazil, due to its unequal access to healthcare services and the lack of training among healthcare professionals to identify the various symptoms [ 23 ]. Despite the existence of a public Unified Health System, important inequalities in access to quality healthcare persist, with the North and Northeast regions lagging behind [ 24 ]. Socioeconomic and educational disparities also remain throughout the country. Our finding that schooling and wealth are positively associated with the number of reported symptoms may be related to greater access to healthcare, but may also be due to recall bias, with poor and uneducated individuals being less likely to recognize symptoms and to report them retrospectively.

Our findings showed that all the symptoms reported were more prevalent in individuals with a history of COVID-19, particularly memory loss, loss of sensitivity in the hands, hair loss, anosmia, and concentration difficulties. The literature in this area is still limited and the lack of standardized diagnostic protocols may hinder future comparisons [ 23 ]. Additionally, delays in consultations and testing due to the overload of the healthcare system hinder more timely care. Furthermore, low public awareness of PCC makes diagnosis and management even more difficult.

PCC has put pressure on healthcare systems. There is an increased need for condition management, both individually and at the societal level. More significant functional limitations in daily activities have been reported in PCC individuals [ 22 ]. This increase in functional limitations may also explain the higher utilization of healthcare services at the primary care level [ 25 ]. The Pan American Health Organization has released a document for reorganizing healthcare systems in four strategic action lines: transforming healthcare systems based on a primary healthcare approach; strengthening leadership, management, and governance; strengthening health service networks; and increasing and sustaining healthcare and social protection funding [ 26 ].

Despite the rigorous methods with which this survey was conducted, some limitations must be considered when interpreting the results. The study sample was based on sentinel cities, which as usually larger and more developed; in rural areas, different findings may be observed. Also, there was an underrepresentation of people <19 years old and those with White skin colour [ 12 ]. Although the weighting considered sex, age, and skin colour strata, the extrapolation of results to the entire Brazilian population and its regions should be done cautiously. The history of COVID-19 was based on self-reporting; testing for COVID-19 in Brazil was challenging and COVID-19 episodes may be underestimated. Another important point is the potential for survival bias. More severe cases may have already resulted in death, underestimating the occurrence of symptoms and PCC.

Our study provides a broad view of how PCC and related symptoms occur in the country. Our findings may help policymakers to design policies and actions for those with a higher number of symptoms, such as women and Indigenous people. Future research should aim for more diverse samples to understand better the long-term consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil and worldwide.
